rv.q: It’s a lovely Chicago play, brought thrillingly back to Broadway life.
A quietly transfixing performance from Ayo Edebiri provides reason enough to see the Broadway revival of "Proof."
Yet, because Edebiri simply doesn’t work as the lead, this revival doesn’t quite knock it out of the park.
Add to that Edebiri, who, while not giving the career-defining performance Parker did, is nonetheless worth seeing.
Edebiri, on the other hand, plays Catherine as a sane but furious woman under a terrific tension, a level of silent agitation that we see even when she turns away.
Despite that strong support, though, it ultimately falls on Edebiri to hold the play’s center of gravity.
It gets where it needs to go; what it lacks, at least for now, is elegance.
As it is, the show comes off lumpy and soft, with the inelegancies of the text left exposed and its sharper points insufficiently filed.
Proof, 25 years later, pulls us in and grips us in a manner that might surprise even the author.
And so will everyone else who comes to see this stunning revival.
An altogether first-class production that speaks to the brain and the heart in equal measure, a winner in every way.
Broadway just got smarter and deeper thanks to the return of David Auburn’s Proof, a complex, curvy, and thoroughly compelling play motored by a math-related mystery.
The piece, by David Auburn, is timeless in its storytelling and still pulls at the heartstrings a quarter of a century after its debut.
Auburn pulls us instantly into this unfamiliar world of college mathematicians and makes us care about these people from the beginning.
Whatever its weaknesses, Proof towers over most of the maladroit star vehicles Broadway has seen recently.
It's the casting that helps bring 'Proof' genuinely up to date.
Her mix of physical comedy, well-timed quips, and heartbreaking reveals must be seen to be believed.
More a competent production than a revelatory one.
A precise but passionless Proof.
There’s a big hole in the middle of this “Proof.”
But Kail’s spiritless revival fails to tap into the play’s specific collision of expansive ideas and fervid emotion.
This formidable production to reveal the terrific twists and turns as they happen.
Auburn’s drama remains a sturdily constructed mystery that deepens as it progresses.
If Proof is a play that explores the relationship between extreme intelligence and mental illness, we must believe Catherine and Robert have both.
Broadway’s first revival of Proof brings the star wattage, but can’t find the current running through David Auburn’s play.
Kail’s revival demonstrates both the durability and the limits of Auburn’s drama.

cn.t: Edebiri earns widespread praise for her captivating Broadway debut in this well-crafted revival, though some critics find the production underpowered and question whether Auburn's Pulitzer winner fully holds up 25 years later.
